title: Is high fructose corn syrup bad for you?
summary: Josh and Chuck, with guest producer Matt filling in for Jerry, explain high fructose corn syrup (HFCS): how enzymes convert glucose into fructose in corn syrup (developed around 1957, perfected and made cheaper in the 1970s), its roughly 10 percent extra fructose compared with table sugar, and how the US farm bill's corn subsidies make corn cheap and abundant. They discuss the rise of HFCS in processed foods, rising US sweetener consumption and obesity and type two diabetes rates, why the liver metabolizes fructose differently (turning excess into triglycerides), and how fructose doesn't trigger ghrelin satiety signals. They close with advice to avoid packaged foods, a cost argument about poorer people eating processed food, a plug for the Super Stuff Guide to the Economy, and a listener sonnet from Daniel in Colorado.

entities.name: Super Stuff Guide to the Economy

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction
segments.summary: Hosts open with a riff on a commercial touting high fructose corn syrup, introduce the topic, and welcome guest producer Matt filling in for Jerry.

segments.title: What HFCS is and its history
segments.summary: HFCS was developed around 1957 when researchers added enzymes to convert glucose in corn syrup into fructose. Fructose is a sweet simple sugar that dissolves better in water. The process was costly until the 1970s, when it was perfected and made cheaper. HFCS contains about 10 percent more fructose than table sugar (sucrose).

segments.title: Farm bill, corn surplus and food aid
segments.summary: The US farm bill gives money to corn producers, leading to corn overproduction and abundance. Surplus corn that once went to Africa as food aid was diverted into syrup production after the 1970s. Hosts note concerns that corn may be used for ethanol instead of food.

segments.title: Spread of HFCS into processed foods and rising consumption
segments.summary: After the 1970s HFCS spread into nearly all foods, including crackers and meats as a preservative. Consumption figures show sucrose's share of US sweetener falling sharply while HFCS rose, and around 2005 Americans consumed 42 pounds of HFCS per person. Public concern grew as type two diabetes and obesity rose.

segments.title: Why fructose is metabolized differently
segments.summary: Unlike glucose, which almost every cell can use, fructose is metabolized mainly by the liver, which has a limit; excess is converted into triglycerides. Ghrelin signals fullness, but fructose does not trigger it, so people may keep eating. Taste of sweeteners also encourages more eating.

segments.title: Avoiding packaged foods and cost argument
segments.summary: Hosts advise checking packaging and avoiding packaged foods. A friend controlled high blood pressure through a fresh-food diet. They argue that HFCS is cheaper than sugar, so processed foods are cheap and poorer people may be more malnourished, though healthy food costs more.

segments.title: Plug for Super Stuff Guide to the Economy
segments.summary: Hosts promote the Super Stuff Guide to the Economy, available on iTunes for four dollars.

segments.title: Listener sonnet from Daniel
segments.summary: Hosts read a sonnet sent by seventeen-year-old Daniel in Colorado praising the free podcast, and invite listeners to send mail to the show's address.
